articles.body:
South Africa

Tributes have been pouring in for South Africa's first female deputy president, Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, who has died at the age of 71.

A statement from her family said she passed away on Friday following complications from a medical procedure she underwent about two weeks ago.

She served as South Africa's deputy president from 2005 to 2008, having previously worked as minerals and energy minister.

The former deputy VP also had stints as United Nations under-secretary-general and headed its agency for gender equality, UN Women, from 2013 to 2021.

She has been praised for her decades-long work on social justice as well as the rights of women.

"Our hearts are really, really sad and broken for having lost such a very dynamic woman leader in our country," President Cyril Ramaphosa said.

"She truly flew the flag of women, not only women of South Africa and Africa, but women of the world," he said.

In a statement on X, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres praised Mlambo-Ngcuka as a "lifelong champion of the rights & empowerment of women and girls".

She "believed that gender equality is not a favour to be granted, but a right to be claimed", he said.

UN Women also paid tribute, lauding her courage and leadership, saying she inspired people around the world.

UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed recalled Mlambo-Ngcuka’s interventions on behalf of women and girls in Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Nigeria.

"She pushed the limits and I think that that's where we got a lot of the confidence to do the things that we do, following in her footsteps," she said.

South African parliamentary officials, unions, and political parties have all been among those expressing their condolences.

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.summary: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
articles.preview: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt. Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty. Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
articles.body:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.

Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.

"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."

The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.

PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.

PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.

Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.

Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.

Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark.

Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

articles.title: Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says
articles.summary: Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south. In a speech on the eve of Lebanon's 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun vowed to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control. Lebanon's sovereignty still faces two threats, he said: "The Israeli occupation of parts of our territory" and foreign interference from "influential elements within the Iranian regime" through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state. On Israel, Aoun stressed Lebanon's message was clear and direct: "Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks." There would be "no occupation ever again", he said. "And no weapons outside the state that... serve the interests of, foreign powers," he added, without naming a specific group. Such weapons may once have served a purpose, he said, but later imposed a high cost on Lebanon when they came to serve causes beyond its borders. "You must hand over your weapons," Aoun said. The Lebanese government has committed to disarming Hezbollah, whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and which has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel. In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement that included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies in the south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area. But implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has refused to surrender its weapons. Israel's army still carries out strikes, shelling and detonations in the south, where its forces are operating in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres. Report by AFP

Such weapons may once have served a purpose, he said, but later imposed a high cost on Lebanon when they came to serve causes beyond its borders.

"You must hand over your weapons," Aoun said. The Lebanese government has committed to disarming Hezbollah, whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and which has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel. articles.title: Allarme voli negli Stati Uniti per il Thanksgiving, 'al Qaida pronta a colpire'

articles.body:
E' massima allerta negli aeroporti degli Stati Uniti alla vigilia della settimana del Thanksgiving, la più trafficata dell'anno. I servizi di intelligence americana hanno notato un aumento di messaggi di Al Qaida e gruppi affiliati sul web che incitano ad emulare l'attentato al volo Flydubai diretto a Tel Aviv dello scorso settembre.

Fbi, dipartimento per la Sicurezza Interna e Transportation Security Administration hanno subito messo in guardia le compagnie aeree commerciali, i vettori cargo e gli aeroporti di tutto il Paese avvertendo che questi messaggi "lodano il dirottamento", per fortuna fallito, "e incoraggiano azioni simili contro obiettivi d'interesse americano, israeliano o ebraico".

Le agenzie hanno quindi esortato gli operatori del settore aereo ad incrementare le normali misure di sicurezza, prestando più attenzione a comportamenti sospetti - come passeggeri che tentano di evitare i controlli o che insistono per gestire personalmente determinati bagagli - e segnalando l'eventuale assenza di tesserini identificativi, uniformi o apparecchi radio. E' stata anche aumentata la presenza di agenti di polizia e unità cinofile.

Al momento non vi sono minacce specifiche e credibili in corso. Ma l'allerta arriva a ridosso della settimana in cui si registra il maggior numero di viaggi in aereo. Secondo l'ente dell'aviazione nazionale si prevede che tra il 24 e il 30 novembre circa 6 milioni di persone si sposteranno su voli interni negli Stati Uniti. Nel documento che l'intelligence americana ha inviato alle compagnie si sottolinea che "i recenti messaggi diffusi dal gruppo terroristico "ribadiscono le narrazioni di lunga data di Al Qaida, che incoraggiano i sostenitori a sfruttare l'accesso al settore dell'aviazione, eludere le misure di sicurezza e compiere attacchi utilizzando aerei commerciali". "Sebbene in passato i soggetti ispirati da organizzazioni terroristiche straniere non si siano mobilitati verso dopo gli appelli all'azione lanciati da tali organizzazioni", si legge nell'avviso diramato al settore dell'aviazione - "essi hanno dimostrato la capacità di mobilitarsi rapidamente, con scarso o nullo preavviso".

Il rapporto ribadisce ancora una volta che il recente plauso espresso da affiliati a gruppi terroristici in merito al tentativo di attacco contro la compagnia Flydubai, soprattutto se unito alle ostilità in corso in Medio Oriente, "potrebbe esacerbare i risentimenti già esistenti nei confronti degli Stati Uniti" e spingere i simpatizzanti dei terroristi a ricorrere alla violenza.

articles.title: Attacco a Bondi beach, due soccorritori si sposano sulla stessa spiaggia
articles.summary: L'amore tra James McIntosh e Alexandra Edmondson è sbocciato all'indomani del massacro
articles.preview: Due soccorritori che contribuirono a salvare le vittime del massacro di Hanukkah a Bondi Beach, in Australia, sono tornati sul luogo ieri per sposarsi nel corso di una cerimonia all'aperto, affacciata sulla spiaggia di Sydney dove la loro relazione era nata proprio all'indomani dell'attacco terroristico. articles.body:
Due soccorritori che contribuirono a salvare le vittime del massacro di Hanukkah a Bondi Beach, in Australia, sono tornati sul luogo ieri per sposarsi nel corso di una cerimonia all'aperto, affacciata sulla spiaggia di Sydney dove la loro relazione era nata proprio all'indomani dell'attacco terroristico. Lo riporta il Times of Israel.

James "Jimmy" McIntosh, 47 anni, e Alexandra "Lexi" Edmondson, 36 anni, si sono scambiati le promesse nuziali ad Archer Park, a North Bondi.

Secondo quanto riportato dai media australiani, circa 200 persone hanno preso parte alla cerimonia, riunendo le famiglie e gli amici della coppia insieme a membri della comunità di Bondi che avevano conosciuto dopo l'attentato, tra cui sopravvissuti, familiari delle vittime e colleghi soccorritori.

Quando l'attacco terroristico ebbe inizio il 14 dicembre 2025 McIntosh ed Edmondson, nessuno dei quali è ebreo, si trovavano nelle vicinanze, diretti a una festa di Natale in un club di surfisti. I due, che a quel tempo si conoscevano solo per aver frequentato un corso di salvataggio, aveva inizialmente cercato riparo, per poi unirsi ai soccorritori una volta cessata la sparatoria.

articles.title: Alta tensione nel mar Baltico, colpita una nave cargo russa
articles.summary: Il premier finlandese: 'La guerra si estende'. Mosca attacca un mercantile a sud di Odessa
articles.preview: Tra i fronti caldi della guerra che contrappone Russia e Ucraina torna a farsi incandescente quello dei mari. Anche se l'episodio che più ha alimentato le tensioni nelle ultime ore è avvenuto molto più a nord rispetto al solito: l'area interessata infatti non è il Mar Nero bensì il golfo di Finlandia, dove la nave Sparta II, un cargo russo salpato venerdì sera da San Pietroburgo in direzione Kaliningrad, è stato colpito poche ore dopo da droni "in acque internazionali, a tre miglia nautiche dal confine russo", secondo le autorità della regione di…
articles.body:
Tra i fronti caldi della guerra che contrappone Russia e Ucraina torna a farsi incandescente quello dei mari. Anche se l'episodio che più ha alimentato le tensioni nelle ultime ore è avvenuto molto più a nord rispetto al solito: l'area interessata infatti non è il Mar Nero bensì il golfo di Finlandia, dove la nave Sparta II, un cargo russo salpato venerdì sera da San Pietroburgo in direzione Kaliningrad, è stato colpito poche ore dopo da droni "in acque internazionali, a tre miglia nautiche dal confine russo", secondo le autorità della regione di Leningrado.

Il raid sul mercantile, attualmente soggetto a sanzioni Usa, è stato confermato da Helsinki, i cui vertici militari ritengono "probabile" la mano ucraina dietro l'attacco. Denunciando anche una "presunta violazione" del proprio spazio aereo da parte di un elicottero russo forse impegnato in "operazioni di salvataggio o sorveglianza" legate proprio alla situazione dello Sparta II.

"La guerra si sta estendendo alle nostre immediate vicinanze", ha commentato il premier finlandese, Petteri Orpo, aggiungendo di ritenere che l'Ucraina ha il diritto di combattere contro l'aggressore". Anche se Kiev, al momento, ha evitato di rivendicare direttamente l'attacco. Sempre secondo le autorità finlandesi, il mercantile nell'attacco "ha subito danni" e a bordo ci sarebbe stato anche un incendio. Una versione non confermata dalle autorità russe. "Secondo quanto riferito dall'equipaggio, non è stata necessaria l'evacuazione", ha sostenuto su Telegram il governatore dell'oblast di Leningrado, Aleksandr Drozdenko, che pur in un primo momento aveva affermato il contrario. "La situazione a bordo è sotto controllo", ha aggiunto Drozdenko, annunciando che era già stata prevista "la ripresa della navigazione" del cargo "lungo la rotta prevista". Versioni contrastanti sono emerse anche rispetto al carico dello Sparta II.

Da un lato una fonte non specificata citata dalla Tass ha indicato che stava trasportando "vernici e smalti". Dall'altro, ci sono informazioni attribuite ai servizi di intelligence statunitensi e ucraini secondo cui questa nave è abitualmente impiegata per trasportare armi. Nelle ore successive all'attacco, il Cremlino è rimasto in silenzio sulla vicenda, almeno pubblicamente. Mentre è stato esplicito nel dar conto delle ultime operazioni condotte dalle forze armate russe: tra queste, un raid per colpire a sud di Odessa, nel Mar Nero, una nave cargo che sarebbe utilizzata da Kiev "per scopi militari" e un attacco contro una stazione elettrica nella città di Vinnytsia.

Intanto, a Kiev il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha incontrato il segretario di Stato britannico alla Difesa, Wes Streeting, soffermandosi poi a parlare con giornalisti sui negoziati per una soluzione al conflitto. Pur ribadendo che per l'Ucraina l'adesione alla Nato resterebbe "la via maestra", il leader di Kiev ha ammesso che al momento tale esito resta "incerto", in quanto non è chiaro come e quando si concluderà la guerra. E ha aggiunto che gli Usa puntano a organizzare un nuovo trilaterale con Ucraina e Russia "entro Natale", dicendosi pronto a partecipare anche se si decidessero di organizzarlo "a livello di leader" a margine del G20 del 14-15 dicembre a Miami.

Al momento, ha tuttavia precisato Zelensky, l'Ucraina non è stata invitata a questo vertice. Intanto non si fermano i raid russi su Kiev, con alcuni quartieri rimasti senza acqua, e su altri centri ucraini tra cui Kryvyi Rih, città natale di Zelensky. Colpito anche un asilo nido a Zaporizhzhia, mentre decine di villaggi sono senza corrente elettrica. Le forze ucraine hanno invece lanciato una nuova ondata di droni verso diverse regioni della Russia, tra cui quella di Leningrado.

articles.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone attack on the vessel.
articles.preview: A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say. The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment. "War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said.
articles.body:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

articles.body:
The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.

The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.

His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.

Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.

The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.

After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.

The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.

Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.

A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters hit the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.

Four Mexican army infantry soldiers died in the operation, the defence ministry said in a statement posted on X that extended the institution’s condolences to their families.

It added that security forces killed seven attackers and arrested eight alleged criminals in the operation, including three who were transferred to Mexico City and five who were turned over to the attorney general’s office in Culiacán, Sinaloa.

Overnight on Friday the military operation triggered a wave of violence in the state of Sinaloa, including armed clashes between Mexican security forces and cartel members, who set up flaming roadblocks in some areas.

By Saturday the violence had substantially subsided. Sinaloa state authorities said “the situation is under control and being addressed by all levels of government”.

Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.

In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.

He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations, and use and possession of a firearm in the US, and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

articles.summary: The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.
articles.preview: November 21, 2026 The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea. Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.
articles.body:
November 21, 2026

The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.

What do we know?

Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials said.

Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.

Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.

Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.

What are the other latest developments?

Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia also struck a cargo vessel near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods for the Ukrainian military.

Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday.

One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.

In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity."

After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway."

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
articles.preview: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine. In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz: Athlete swims through war zone to expose war's environmental toll
articles.summary: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh completed a 15-kilometre swim through the Strait of Hormuz over three days in November 2026, braving explosions and burning tankers nearby. His three-day challenge aimed to expose the environmental damage caused by the war with Iran.
articles.preview: Wearing nothing but swimming trunks, goggles and a UN-branded cap, 56-year-old ocean campaigner Lewis Pugh entered the waters off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, where he found himself swimming within sight of burning ships and towering plumes of smoke. articles.body: Wearing nothing but swimming trunks, goggles and a UN-branded cap, 56-year-old ocean campaigner Lewis Pugh entered the waters off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, where he found himself swimming within sight of burning ships and towering plumes of smoke. Just 20 minutes into his first swim, two explosions rocked the area and an oil tanker caught fire around four kilometres away, forcing him to abandon the attempt temporarily. The following day, he witnessed another vessel engulfed in flames as he continued his swim through the strategic waterway. A United Nations Patron of the Oceans, Pugh warned that pollution from damaged tankers could devastate coral reefs, mangroves and coastal ecosystems for decades. Yet sightings of dolphins, turtles and ospreys reminded him of the extraordinary wildlife at risk. Having previously swum in the Arctic, Antarctic and Red Sea to raise awareness of ocean conservation, he delivered a stark appeal: “We’ve got to stop the war. We’ve got to open the strait, and we’ve got to clean up this mess.”

articles.title: Around 700,000 displaced by volatile conflict in southern Ethiopia
articles.summary: NGO Islamic Relief says fighting between ethnic groups competing for land and wealth has seen widespread destruction of homes and disruption of services.
articles.preview: Ethiopia British NGO Islamic Relief says fighting sparked by a dispute over who controls the southern town of Moyale on Ethiopia’s border with Kenya has seen around 700,000 people displaced from their homes. It said on Thursday that clashes between members of the Oromo and Ethiopian Somali communities began in late October. Fighting involving heavy weaponry has now reportedly spread up to 300 kilometres from the town along the Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopian border.
articles.body:
Ethiopia

British NGO Islamic Relief says fighting sparked by a dispute over who controls the southern town of Moyale on Ethiopia’s border with Kenya has seen around 700,000 people displaced from their homes.

It said on Thursday that clashes between members of the Oromo and Ethiopian Somali communities began in late October.

Fighting involving heavy weaponry has now reportedly spread up to 300 kilometres from the town along the Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopian border.

"This is a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in the borders of Ethiopia," said Kedir Musema Hameza, the head of Islamic Relief's Ethiopia programme.

The NGO said there has been widespread destruction of homes, businesses, and petrol stations, as well as disruption of essential services, including health, water, and sanitation.

It said access to the locations has been challenging and warns of a deepening humanitarian crisis.

Approximately 50,000 people have fled into Kenya placing additional pressure on local services and host communities.

The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who hails from the Oromia region, has not commented on the violence.

The borders between the country's regions, set by the 1995 constitution, have been a frequent source of conflict in Ethiopia which currently faces multiple internal conflicts.

Just weeks ago, fighting erupted in Tigray, hundreds of kilometres to the north, when rebels and government forces clashed.

There have also been long-running insurgencies in the most populous regions of Amhara and Oromia that have displaced hundreds of thousands.

articles.title: ‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges

articles.preview: Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.

articles.summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran wanted guarantees that Washington was serious about negotiations before proceeding further.
articles.preview: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its war with the United States, while U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran wanted a deal but one that was not acceptable to him. Araqchi told the state-owned Iran newspaper that messages continued to be exchanged between Iran and Washington through mediators, and that Tehran was seeking “an agreement that would ensure there was no further war.” He also said Iran wanted guarantees that Washington was serious about negotiations before proceeding further, adding that Iran…
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its war with the United States, while U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran wanted a deal but one that was not acceptable to him.

Araqchi told the state-owned Iran newspaper that messages continued to be exchanged between Iran and Washington through mediators, and that Tehran was seeking “an agreement that would ensure there was no further war.”

He also said Iran wanted guarantees that Washington was serious about negotiations before proceeding further, adding that Iran had discussed with mediators the form and nature of confidence-building measures.

The remarks came as diplomatic efforts continued to try to end a conflict that has destabilized the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices and drawn in countries across the region.

The foreign minister said Iran’s red lines included keeping its highly enriched uranium in the country, though he said a “fair solution” was still possible.

Authorities have previously mentioned “feasible formulas” to resolve the dispute between Tehran and Washington over the matter, including diluting the highly enriched uranium stockpile under the supervision of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The IAEA estimates that Iran had 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the U.S. attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.

“I believe a fair solution can be reached on the issue of nuclear material, one that is based on our national interests while also meeting the country’s needs,” Araqchi said.

Trump, in a bews conference on Friday, said: “They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me.”

The United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to strike Israel and Gulf states hosting U.S. military bases.

Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday in talks aimed at “bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground,” a spokesperson for Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said.

articles.body:
THE HAGUE – The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya will strengthen South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza, legal experts said, establishing a precedent that genocidal intent can coexist with a military objective.

While the conflicts in Gaza and Myanmar are legally distinct, both cases before the World Court are based on allegations that states breached their obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

On Thursday, the court found that Myanmar had violated the convention on multiple grounds stemming from mistreatment of the Muslim Rohingya minority by the armed forces.

articles.title: A tale of two Nvidias
articles.summary: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia — the company’s latest earnings report vs. the tech executives loudly calling for Jensen Huang’s return.
articles.preview: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.
articles.body:
We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.

And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.

Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.

It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”

So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

Kirsten: Sure, never say never.

Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.

Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

articles.title: Il Ceo di Anthropic in Puglia, forse a un evento sull'IA di una società italiana

articles.preview: Il ceo di Anthropic, Dario Amodei, che ieri mattina è atterrato a Brindisi, starebbe partecipando a un evento organizzato da una società italiana di consulenza e servizi informatici nel resort Borgo Egnazia, a Fasano. articles.body:
Il ceo di Anthropic, Dario Amodei, che ieri mattina è atterrato a Brindisi, starebbe partecipando a un evento organizzato da una società italiana di consulenza e servizi informatici nel resort Borgo Egnazia, a Fasano. L'azienda, a quanto si apprende, si occupa, tra l'altro, di intelligenza artificiale e analisi dei dati, cloud e infrastrutture digitali, e cybersecurity.

"Per noi - spiega all'ANSA il sindaco di Fasano, Francesco Zaccaria - essere diventati un punto di riferimento, ogni giorno, per gente che arriva da ogni parte del mondo, ci riempie chiaramente di orgoglio e soprattutto ripaga il lavoro svolto negli ultimi anni. La consacrazione del G7 ci ha permesso di mostrare al mondo la nostra parte migliore del nostro territorio".

Continuano intanto a circolare le ipotesi di un suo possibile investimento immobiliare. Nell'ultimo anno alcuni suoi stretti collaboratori avrebbero più volte visitato la Puglia per valutare l'acquisto di una lussuosa masseria. Mentre un'altra possibile operazione potrebbe riguardare l'acquisto, per il quale ci sarebbero trattative in corso, di un resort situato tra le province di Bari e Brindisi.

"Certo siamo tutti contenti che lui è qui, ma - sottolinea il sindaco di Brindisi Pino Marchionna - è in forma assolutamente privata. Ho avuto modo di parlare anche con altre autorità che non erano state informate in quanto lui è sceso come un privato cittadino, è arrivato con un volo diretto da New York, ha fatto i controlli di frontiera come qualunque cittadino normale e noi dobbiamo rispettare la privacy di questa persona". "Ci fa molto piacere che personaggi di tale caratura, all'indomani di una performance straordinaria sul piano borsistico - conclude - abbiano scelto la provincia di Brindisi, il nostro aeroporto, dopo momenti di grande stress".

articles.title: After outages hit US banks and aviation, FBI database reported hacked
articles.summary: After outages hit US banks and aviation, FBI database reported hacked Submitted by MEE staff on Sat, 11/21/2026 - 14:57 The database holds information on warrants and identities of fugitives, with experts warning that hackers could alter records relied on by police FBI director Kash Patel is sworn in before testifying at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, 15 September 2026 (Roberto Schmidt/AFP) Off The FBI is investigating a breach of its nationwide criminal information database, reported after a series of major technology disruptions in recent weeks. The intrusion into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which federal, state and local law enforcement agencies use to share criminal justice information, was discovered in recent days, CNN reported . The FBI has called it a central law enforcement information system used by agencies across the country. The potential consequences extend beyond the theft of sensitive information. A former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups said that officers rely on the database to identify fugitives, check outstanding warrants and access information. “My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on,” the former official told CNN. FBI director Kash Patel addressed the bureau's cybersecurity efforts on Fox News on Thursday, after officials had learned of the latest intrusion. articles.body:
For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.

The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.

Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”

Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.

Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.

The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.

This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.

In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”

Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”

But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?

Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.

Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.

A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”

Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”

How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.

A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”

For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.

Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.

“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”

Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.

Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.

Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”
